nameStory: The Hartford fern gets its name from Hartford, Connecticut, where it once grew abundantly in the surrounding area. Early settlers in the Hartford region were so enchanted by this delicate climbing fern that they harvested it extensively as Christmas decorations, leading to the first plant protection law in the United States in 1869.
description: Hartford fern is New England's only native climbing fern, creating delicate green curtains as it twines up through shrubs and small trees. Unlike typical ferns that grow in clumps, this one sends out thin, wiry stems that can climb several feet high, producing small, palm-shaped leaflets along the way. The whole plant has an airy, lace-like appearance that sets it apart from any other fern you'll encounter in New England.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Thin, wiry black stems that climb and twine through other plants like a delicate green vine, unlike any other New England fern

idTips.label: Fronds
idTips.description: Small, palm-shaped leaflets about the size of a quarter, each divided into 4-7 finger-like lobes that feel thin and papery

idTips.label: Stipe
idTips.description: Very thin, dark brown to black stem that feels tough and wiry, almost like fine wire covered in bark

idTips.label: Sori
idTips.description: Spores form on specialized fertile leaflets that look different from regular ones, with narrow, finger-like segments that feel slightly thicker

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Always in very wet, acidic spots with bright sunlight - often the only fern thriving in sunny, boggy openings

habitat: Hartford fern requires a very specific combination of constant moisture, bright sunlight, and intensely acidic soil. Look for it in sunny wetlands, bog edges, and wet meadows where few other plants can tolerate the harsh conditions. It often grows in sphagnum moss or other acid-loving plants in areas that stay soggy year-round.

seasonality.spring: New climbing stems emerge and begin their upward journey, looking fresh green and delicate as they unfurl their first palm-shaped leaflets.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season when the climbing stems reach their full height and the distinctive palm-shaped leaflets are most visible throughout the plant.
seasonality.fall: Fertile leaflets produce spores before the entire plant begins to die back, turning brown and becoming less noticeable.
seasonality.winter: Stems die back to ground level, leaving little visible trace until spring emergence.

funFact: This rare fern was so beloved as Christmas decoration by early New England settlers that it became the very first plant species to receive legal protection in American history - Connecticut passed a law in 1869 specifically to save the Hartford fern from over-collection!
confusionNotes: The climbing habit makes this impossible to confuse with any other fern in New England - it's the only one that acts like a vine. Young plants before they start climbing might be mistaken for small woodland ferns, but the distinctive palm-shaped leaflets with finger-like lobes are unique.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called Hartford fern after Hartford, Connecticut, this species has become extremely rare throughout New England and is listed as endangered or threatened in several states. Its populations are described as 'abundant but rare' - meaning where you do find it, there's often a lot of it, but those spots are few and far between.
compareHints: Hartford fern is the only climbing fern species native to North America, making it unique in its genus here. While there are other climbing ferns in the world (like the invasive Japanese climbing fern found in the Southeast), none others occur in New England. This gives our Hartford fern the distinction of being completely one-of-a-kind in our region.
